idiom_name: ensure + block form of the acquiring method (File.open { }) - finalizers only as a net
implementation_notes: Ruby has no destructors and no Dispose contract, so the pattern appears as two local idioms: an explicit close method invoked inside an ensure clause (which runs on exceptions and early returns alike), and the block form of the acquiring method - File.open(path) { |f| ... }, IO.pipe, Tempfile.create - where the method itself guarantees release after the block. The block form is the idiomatic replacement for the classic acquire/use/release call sequence; it is not a syntax feature but an API convention the stdlib follows consistently. Ownership and idempotence remain the implementer's job: an owner class cascades to its own resources inside close. ObjectSpace.define_finalizer exists for objects wrapping native resources, but the documentation presents it as an MRI-level facility and it runs late (at GC) with no ordering guarantees, so it cannot replace ensure/close.
code_sketch:
class Session
  def initialize(conn) = (@conn, @closed = conn, false)
  def close                              # idempotent cascade
    (@closed = true) && @conn.close unless @closed
  end
end
def handle
  s = Session.new(connect)
  s.round_trip
ensure
  s.close                                # runs on exceptions and normal return
end
pitfalls: An exception raised inside the ensure clause masks the original one; rescue around the release when cleanup can fail.

ObjectSpace.define_finalizer is not a Dispose substitute: it fires at an unspecified GC point, its callback receives only the object id, and the docs discourage using it for ordinary resource management.
Block-form methods release only for block callers - passing the object out of the block or using the non-block form silently opts out of the guarantee, so prefer the block form at every call site.
